*Overview of section 8, version 0.3, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author's own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. This overview replaces the combined overview and the overview of additional papers (versions 0.1 and 0.2), both in `8.0.Overview/8.PreviousVersions`. The research page is at https://climatefiscalfinance.org/research.html.*

# Why these papers sit outside the active sections {.unnumbered}

Moving a paper here is a statement about attention, not quality. Some retained work has been overtaken by later papers in the active sections. Some is an argument with no draft behind it yet. Some is a framework kept because later papers draw on it. What these papers have in common is that they are not under active development, and a research page that did not say so would mislead the reader about where the work is going.

The section is numbered by subject. Its subsections follow the active sections they relate to (8.1 fiscal policy, 8.2 finance and risk, 8.3 sovereign incentives and the development banks, 8.4 analytics), then the books (8.5), philosophy (8.6) and politics (8.7). A paper brought back into an active section takes that section's next number.

# Retained papers {.unnumbered}

**8.1.1 Stranded by Contract: Reforming Legacy Coal Power Purchase Agreements.** A coal plant can be stranded in economic terms while its contract keeps the money flowing. Where the variable cost of coal generation exceeds the all-in cost of new solar, the distribution company pays more under a legacy power purchase agreement than it would pay to replace the plant outright, so retiring the plant and buying solar power instead saves money before any climate benefit is counted. The folder holds India country material but no paper yet. It relates to the rent and fiscal work of section 2.

**8.2.1 The Sollar.** The other mechanisms in the finance papers make borrowers creditworthy; the Sollar removes the borrower. One Sollar is an undivided share in a portfolio of utility-scale solar parks in several countries, with electricity revenue reinvested so that the capacity behind each unit grows. A developer can borrow Sollars during construction and repay by issuing them against the finished park, financing the asset with a claim on what it will produce rather than with debt. The paper sets out the design and what it does not solve.

**8.3.2 Reforming MDBs.** Every sovereign incentive instrument in section 4 needs an institution with a balance sheet, a mandate and market credibility. This paper sets out the roles the multilateral development banks, and the World Bank Group in particular, could take in scaling climate action, as lenders and as policy influencers, and the two problems they must solve: scale, and incentives for policy.

**8.4.1 Climate-Fiscal-Financial.** Climate policy settings, fiscal aggregates and financial-sector exposures are assessed by different teams using different data, so nobody sees a country as one balance sheet. This is a planned dashboard that would bring the three onto one country view. There is no draft yet; the folder holds framing material on the scale of the climate finance gap and the instruments that could close it.

**8.4.2 Green Growth and Sectoral TFP Diagnostic.** Countries want green industrial policy but often lack a structured way to pick promising sectors. This planned diagnostic would score which green sectors are feasible targets in a given country and link the scores to total factor productivity accounting. There is no draft yet.

**8.4.3 Carbon Pricing: Political Economy and Optimality.** Climate policy instruments succeed or fail on political fit as well as economic design, and the two questions are usually answered by literatures that never meet. A compact model of global mitigation incentives supplies the benchmark of what policy should be; a six-driver diagnostic of fiscal pressure, political salience, vested interests, distributive design, institutional quality and energy structure asks what a given country can carry. The folder holds the toy model and the policy framework tables; the carbon-pricing papers of section 1 cite the toy model.

# Books {.unnumbered}

**8.5.1 Time and Chance.** A book-length treatment of why clean energy costs too much in the countries that need it most. It runs from the price of money, through contracts as the instrument that makes revenue bankable, to the structures built on them (guarantees, synthetic sovereign bonds, clean energy equity funds and the Sollar), and then to the institutions that would carry them. The finance and sovereign-incentive papers of sections 3 and 4 are the paper-length statements of several of its chapters; where the two differ, the papers are later and should be preferred.

**8.5.2 Carbon Pricing: The Right Policy at the Wrong Time.** Carbon pricing is the right instrument, but the political and financial order in which it would have worked has largely passed. The book takes the argument of the carbon-pricing papers to book length: what a price is for, why the case for it was won intellectually and lost operationally, what open economies can do unilaterally, and which instruments, feebates first, do the work in the interval. Section 1 holds the paper-length versions.

**8.5.3 Screwed?! Getting Our Future Back with Tax and Benefit Reform.** A 2020 book manuscript with Gordon Styles, about 102,000 words in fourteen chapters, making a case for reforming UK tax and benefits: tax principles and practice, welfare and work, inequality, corporations, land and property, money and debt, and environment and resources. It is kept as written in 2020. The Rent Tax paper in section 2 states its land and corporate argument in short form.

# Philosophy {.unnumbered}

Three essays on what happens when a governing metaphor stops being noticed as a metaphor.

**8.6.1 Order Without Ordinance** is a dialogue on the picture of nature as obeying laws, a metaphor that kept the legislation after the Enlightenment removed the legislator, set against the Chinese idea of order that nobody wrote. **8.6.2 The Politics of Life-Logic** reconstructs the critique of a politics that begins by judging life deficient, from Nietzsche through Hayek, Hirschman, Easterly and Scott, draws on Chinese and Indian traditions, and ends in institutional proposals for the World Bank. **8.6.3 The Vocative Case** asks what contemporary atheism is arguing with, and whether religious language was ever the kind of claim that can be refuted.

# Political writing {.unnumbered}

Three pieces written outside the professional portfolio and not offered as research.

**8.7.1 Manifesto for a New American Republic** is a short political statement on defending and then reforming the American constitutional order. **8.7.2 Progressive Collapse of a Uniform Column** derives from first principles the mechanics of a falling upper block in a tall uniform column and applies them to the World Trade Center towers. **8.7.3 Statistical Anomalies, Voting Machines, and the 2024 US Presidential Election** assesses the statistical claims made about the election, explaining each concept and reconstructing an example before judging how strongly it points to manipulation. The last two are methodological exercises on contested subjects, written to establish what the evidence shows and to stop there.
